doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Teaching with the Monterey Jazz Festival education program
summary: Since about 1983 he has been a clinician in the Monterey program started by Jimmy Lyons and Mundell Lowe; also his high school band director Aubrey Pennyman.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I mean you asked me about doing other things, and I’ve sort of avoided the teaching per se. I mean I give an occasional lesson but I don’t have a stable of students or a place. But I am involved and I have been since its inception for twenty years now, in the Monterey Jazz Festival has a jazz educational program that was started oh around ’83 I guess or ’84. Jimmy Lyons, who ran the festival for so many years, he and the then- musical director Mundell Lowe got the idea to put music education in Monterey County which is the home of the Monterey Jazz Festival, as a give back, as a gift. So they started with three clinicians: myself, Bill Berry — have you talked to Bill Berry?

Oh yeah, he’s great. I love Bill Berry. Bill Berry, myself and a very fine musician from the Santa Cruz area named Paul Contos, a reed player, very good. The three of us started. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

And when they tapped me I had worked the festival a few times with Cal Tjader and some other people. And so Jimmy says, “You want to do this thing?” And I said, “I’m not a teacher, I wouldn’t know where to begin.” I mean it’s true, I mean you need an educator. He said, “Nope, Mundell said we want players just to go in and impart your experience.” I said, “Okay I’ll try it.” Twenty years later, you know? It’s fun. I enjoy that. I really do.

Well I think it’s an important thing that teachers of jazz — and I suppose you could say this about anything, but especially of jazz, ought to be players first. And I’m not sure that’s the norm anymore in the universities.

Well universities I don’t know. I don’t spend much time in universities. I go in to just middle schools and high schools, and band directors at most of these places are not jazz musicians. But the high school I went to, the band director was not a jazz musician but he was a good musician and he was very open and he encouraged myself, Rufus Reid, he was a year behind me, Mel Martin — I don’t know if you talked to Mel — and a few other guys that have made a living playing music, went to this school and were lucky enough to be under the tutelage of this man, Aubrey Pennyman, and he wasn’t a jazz musician but he gave us our head. He said, “What do you want to do?” So it can work. But it helps. I wish, like we go into a school and while the band’s rehearsing, and I sidle up next to the drummers and just make friends and they play and then I’ll point something out on the chart or the equipment or it’s like a real hands on, like an hour thing. It’s not a one-on-one private lesson. And then all the time I’m giving him some pointers or I demonstrate. And I wish somebody had done that for me. I mean I didn’t have that benefit. I had to really go find places to watch musicians play.
